title: Only the loudest in each square
allegory: Max pooling is like a scout reporting from a map cut into 2x2 squares: from each square she radios back only the strongest signal, so the map shrinks to a quarter but no strong signal is lost, only its exact spot.
map: a feature map: how strongly a detector fired at each position
one 2x2 square, stepping two squares at a time
a pooling window with kernel 2 and stride 2
radioing back only the strongest signal
taking the max of each window
the scout carries no notebook of weights
no learned parameters, unlike a convolution
only the signal she reported gets thanked afterwards
only the max element receives gradient
credit: The 'was this feature detected anywhere in the window?' reading follows Andrew Ng, Deep Learning Specialization, Convolutional Neural Networks, 'Pooling Layers'.

chapters.name: Too big to carry
chapters.note: most neighbours say the same thing

cap.1: A detector has scored every pixel for 'is there an edge here?'. The map is big, and neighbouring scores mostly say the same thing.
cap.2: After a conv layer each channel is a full-size feature map. You want it smaller before the next layer, without learning anything new to do it.
cap.3: Feature maps are spatially redundant. Downsampling cuts work for later layers and widens each later unit's receptive field, and a fixed rule can do it with zero parameters.

cap.1: A scout crosses a map cut into small squares. From each square she radios back one number: the strongest signal in it. The map shrinks, the peaks survive.
cap.2: Max pooling slides a window, usually 2x2 with stride 2, across the map and outputs each window's maximum. Height and width halve; three of every four numbers are dropped.
cap.3: MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2): non-overlapping windows, output = window max. It keeps the strongest activation per region and forgets where inside the window it was.

chapters.name: Four squares, four winners
chapters.title: 4x4 in, 2x2 out: keep each square's max

cap.1: Sixteen numbers, four 2x2 squares. The lit cell in each square is its biggest number, and only those four go on to the next layer.
cap.2: Each 2x2 window reports its max: 5, 6, 6, 5. The output is 2x2. The other twelve values are simply not passed on.
cap.3: Input (4, 4), output (2, 2): out[i, j] = max over x[2i:2i+2, 2j:2j+2]. Twelve of sixteen activations are discarded; the backward pass only needs the argmax positions.

cap.1: Each output cell is the biggest number in its own little square. Step two cells, take the max, repeat. There is nothing to learn.
cap.2: In [0.2] you build it from the stride trick: as_strided makes a view of every 2x2 window without copying, then you take the max over the two window axes.
cap.3: View sizes (B, C, H_out, W_out, k, k) with strides (sB, sC, s·sH, s·sW, sH, sW), then amax over the last two dims. H_out = floor((H + 2p - k)/s + 1), the same formula as conv.

chapters.name: The padding trap

left.title: pad with 0
lines: a value that was never there

chapters.verdict: For a max, padding must be a value that can never win.

cap.1: At the edge the scout counts empty squares too. If empty counts as 0 and every real signal is negative, she reports 0, a signal nobody sent.
cap.2: Padding a max pool with zeros invents values when activations are negative. Pad with -inf so padding can never be the max. nn.MaxPool2d does this for you.
cap.3: Zero padding biases border maxima upward whenever every real value in the window is below 0. The identity for max is -inf, as 0 is for sum: pad with the identity of the reduction.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: nn.MaxPool2d: a library call from here on
Gradient flows only to each window's winner

cap.1: After this exercise it is one library call. Keep the idea: pooling picks, it never learns, and only the winners get credit when the model updates.
cap.2: nn.MaxPool2d from now on. For understanding a model: pooling has no weights, so the learned features live in the convolutions; the pool only selects.
cap.3: Max is piecewise linear, so gradient reaches only each window's argmax: attributions through a pool are sparse and snapped to winners. Learned features live in the kernels, not the pool.

coda.title: Tap cells to raise them and watch the pooled 2x2 report

readouts.label: winners (the only cells that get gradient)

caption.1: Tap a cell to raise it. Raise a small one: the report does not move. Keep going until it beats its square's winner, then watch it take over.
caption.2: Only the max of each 2x2 window survives. Bumping a non-winner changes nothing, which is exactly why its gradient is zero. The winners list is where gradient flows.
caption.3: The output is flat in every non-argmax input (zero gradient) until that input crosses the current max, then tracks it 1:1. Ties aside, each window routes all of dL/dy to one cell.

where_else: Global max pooling: one number per channel saying whether a feature fired anywhere in the image
Max-activating examples for a neuron or SAE latent: the max over positions, 'did it fire anywhere here?'
Greedy decoding: keep the single top-scoring token, drop the rest

hamming.what: A parameter-free way to shrink a feature map by keeping the largest value in each small window.
hamming.when: Between convolution layers in a CNN, when you want smaller maps and do not care exactly where inside a window a feature fired.
hamming.why: The max keeps the strongest evidence that a pattern appeared while cutting the map to a quarter and forgiving small shifts.

object.title: The pooling tray
object.subtitle: A 4x4 tray of bars that collapses to one height per square, where only the tallest bar in each square is wired backwards.
object.f: ((R, C, v) => { const m = Math.max(v(R, C), v(R, C+1), v(R+1, C), v(R+1, C+1)); return view < 0.5 ? v(r, c) : view < 1.5 ? m : (v(r, c) === m ? 1 : 0.05); })(Math.floor(r/2)*2, Math.floor(c/2)*2, (i, j) => ((i*3 + j*5) % 7)/4 + 0.2)

cap.1: Sixteen bars: a detector's scores on a small patch. Tall means it fired strongly there.
cap.2: A 4x4 feature map. Bar height = activation.
cap.3: One channel of a feature map, 4x4, before pooling.

cap.1: Pool: each 2x2 square becomes one flat block, as tall as its tallest bar.
cap.2: Max pool, kernel 2, stride 2: every window collapses to its max. Four values survive.
cap.3: Each plateau is out[i, j] = max over its window, drawn at full size to show which inputs it covers.

cap.1: From above: four squares, four numbers. A quarter of the data, and no peak lost.
cap.2: Height and width halve, so the next layer has a quarter of the positions to process.
cap.3: (4, 4) -> (2, 2). Each surviving value summarises a 2x2 region, so later layers cover more of the image per unit.

cap.1: Now run it backwards. Only the tallest bar in each square still stands: it alone gets the credit or the blame.
cap.2: Backward pass: gradient goes only to each window's argmax. The other twelve get exactly zero.
cap.3: d out / d x is 1 at the argmax and 0 elsewhere in each window: max pooling is a sparse router of gradient.

cap.1: Nudge a short bar up a little and its pooled block would not move. Only the winner matters.
cap.2: Small changes to non-max inputs leave the output alone, and so does moving the peak within its square.
cap.3: Local invariance: the output ignores perturbations below the window max and moves of the max within its window.

predict.q: How many learned weights does a 2x2 max pool have?

options.t: None: it only picks the biggest
Four, one per cell in the window

predict.why: Max pooling is a fixed rule. Convolution is the one with a learned kernel.

predict.q: During backprop, which cells in a 2x2 window get gradient?

options.t: Only the one that was the max

predict.why: Nudging a non-max cell does not change the output, so its gradient is zero. Sharing equally is what average pooling does.

predict.q: You pad with zeros and every real value in an edge window is negative. What does the pool report?

options.t: 0, a value that was never in the data

predict.why: Zero padding can win the max. Pad with -inf so padding never can.

object.where: Anywhere you ask 'did it happen somewhere in this region?': global max pooling, max over positions for max-activating examples.
